title: Short Stuff: What did we use before infant formula?
summary: Short Stuff episode on what people fed infants before modern infant formula, prompted by the 2022 baby formula shortage in the United States. The hosts cover wet nursing from ancient times through its exploitative history and today's casual milk-sharing among friends and family, feeding animal milk (donkey, goat, horse, sheep, pig), and the pap and pap boat (gravy boat) method with its sterilization problems. They then trace formula history: Justus von Liebig's 1865 cow's milk formula, Henri Nestlé's follow-up, the rise of brands, the 1950s liquid formula, and the shift back toward breastfeeding in the 1970s and 80s. They close with the Infant Formula Act of 1980, why formula is heavily regulated and unsafe to make at home, and a note of sympathy for stressed parents.

segments.title: Opening and the formula shortage
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode, noting the stress of the US baby formula shortage and a HowStuffWorks article by Alicia Hoyt. He asks what people used to do when mothers could not breastfeed.

segments.title: Wet nursing
segments.summary: The hosts discuss wet nursing going back about four thousand years, often tied to the elite and sometimes forced on enslaved women, and the exploitative history described in a book on the topic. They note that today milk sharing is usually casual among friends and family, mostly through pumped milk.

segments.title: Animal milk and the pap boat
segments.summary: Without a wet nurse, families used milk from animals such as donkeys, goats, horses, sheep, or pigs. Earlier, starting in the century mentioned, infants were fed pap, a wet cereal or milk toast, using a pap boat, essentially a gravy boat. The main problem was lack of sterilization, which drove infant mortality more than nutrient gaps.

segments.title: Break and TV anecdote
segments.summary: A brief aside in which Josh talks about his daughter watching a TV appearance of his, before the hosts take a break.

segments.title: Early formula: von Liebig and Nestlé
segments.summary: After the break, the hosts describe the first formula attempt in 1865 by Justus von Liebig, made from cow's milk, malt flour, wheat, and potassium bicarbonate. A couple of years later pharmacist Henri Nestlé launched a similar, easier-to-mix product. Within about fifteen years there were nearly thirty infant food brands.

segments.title: Evaporated milk to liquid formula
segments.summary: In the 1930s and 1940s evaporated milk was recommended once safe canning was figured out. The first liquid formula, needing no mixing, came in the early 1950s and was popular with mothers. In the 1970s and 1980s attention returned to breastfeeding, and the hosts link formula's acceptance to feminism and a current non-judgmental attitude toward feeding choices.

segments.title: Why formula cannot be made at home
segments.summary: The hosts explain that infant formula is heavily regulated by the Infant Formula Act, which sets nutrient standards and recall rules, and that it is scientifically calibrated. Experts advise against homemade formula because it cannot match those nutrients and poses a safety risk.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh expresses sympathy for stressed parents and asks listeners to send in tips. The episode closes with the standard credits.
